evidence.label: A closed Ricci flow with bounded scalar curvature and finite-time curvature blowup
Bounded scalar curvature and smooth extension of four-dimensional Ricci flow
Path selection and an elliptic inequality on degenerating Ricci-flat trees

headline: Claims four-dimensional Ricci flow continues while scalar curvature is bounded, but not in some high dimension.
scope: Smooth Ricci flows on closed manifolds. The extension theorem covers real dimension four; the counterexample lives on S² × S^(q+1) for some q ≥ 10.
plain: Ricci flow is an equation that slowly reshapes a curved space, like heat evening out a temperature. It can break down at a finite time, when the curvature becomes infinite somewhere. An old question asks whether the simplest average of curvature, the scalar curvature, must also become infinite there. The papers claim yes for closed four-dimensional spaces and no in some high dimension. There is no Lean check.
doesNot: This does not say what happens in dimensions five up to the dimension of the counterexample. It has no Lean check. The counterexample is only said to exist for some q ≥ 10.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Richard Hamilton, who showed a closed flow stops only when full curvature blows up
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims to settle a central extension question for Ricci flow in dimension four and to disprove its all-dimensions form.

explanation:
Start with a round four-sphere of radius 1. Ricci flow changes a curved space over time, shrinking it where it bends like a sphere. Under the flow the radius squared falls by 6 per unit time, so it equals 1 − 6t. The sphere vanishes at time t = 1/6. Scalar curvature is a single number at each point that averages all the bending. For this sphere it is 12/(1 − 6t). At t = 0 it is 12. At t = 0.15 it is 120. At t = 0.166 it is 3000. So here the scalar curvature blows up exactly when the flow breaks down.

Must this always happen? A smooth Ricci flow on a closed space can stop at a finite time only if its full curvature becomes unbounded[1]. Closed means finite in size with no edge. Full curvature records the bending in every direction, not just the average. The scalar-curvature extension conjecture asks if the average must blow up too[2]. Earlier, Šešum showed that a bound on the Ricci tensor, a middle-sized summary of curvature, is enough[3]. The difficulty is that scalar curvature can vanish in a blow-up limit while the full curvature does not[4]. The limit can then be Ricci-flat, curved but with zero Ricci tensor, without being flat.

The second paper claims a yes in dimension four. A flow on a closed four-manifold extends past any finite time at which scalar curvature stays bounded[5]. Bamler and Zhang had shown this when a certain topological invariant vanishes[6]. At a point where curvature might pile up, rescaling reveals a finite tree of Ricci-flat pieces[7]. The central problem is to stop the outermost piece from shrinking, while smaller pieces inside it may shrink[8]. The third paper supplies a key estimate for a renormalized energy on such trees of Ricci-flat spaces[9].

The first paper claims a no in high dimension. It builds a flow on the product of a two-sphere and a sphere of dimension q + 1, with q at least 10[10]. Its scalar curvature stays bounded, but its full curvature becomes infinite at a finite time[10]. This refutes the conjecture in its form for all dimensions of at least four[11]. It asserts nothing in dimension four[12]. The example builds on Stolarski's flows that form cone-shaped singularities[13]. The new step is a bound on scalar curvature near the tip of the forming cone.

How sure is this? There is no Lean check. A computer proof checker has not looked at any part of it. The four-dimensional proof is long and depends on a companion paper for its key static estimate. No specialist review of the papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proofs hold. There is no Lean check, the four-dimensional proof is long and rests on a companion paper, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: An equation that changes a curved space over time, shrinking it where it bends like a sphere.
One number at each point that averages all the ways the space bends there.
The complete record of how the space bends in every pair of directions.
A summary of curvature between the full record and the single scalar average.
Having zero Ricci tensor; such a space can still be curved.
A space that is finite in size and has no edge.
A time at which the flow cannot continue smoothly because curvature becomes infinite.
